solver.kind: blind AI solver B (separate agent, answer-free packet, adversarial rubric)

flags.note: Choice B is grammatically awkward against the stem: 'anchoring ... is swayed even by irrelevant numbers' makes anchoring the thing that gets swayed, but people are swayed and anchoring is the effect. Suggested fix: 'can arise from even irrelevant numbers and is best countered by changing the starting point.' Also, 'best countered' slightly overstates the passage's 'had more success'; that is acceptable for a main-idea item.

R063-01.notes: A is contradicted by the real estate study (P3), C by 'warning ... done little' (P4), D by the 1970s T&K origin (agents were subjects, not discoverers). B joins the claims in P2 and P5. No real case for any distractor.

R063-02.notes: P1: 65 group median was 45. B (25) is the 10 group swap trap. A and C are the wheel values. The passage matches T&K 1974.

R063-03.notes: Supported by P2, 'need not be relevant ... need not be believed.' B: the participants did understand the number was random. C: the rigging serves the design and is not the point of the phrase. D: no true value is given. A's 'know it is meaningless' fairly paraphrases 'could see was random'. The fact that the wheel was secretly rigged does not undermine this, because participants perceived it as random.

R063-04.notes: Appraisals tracked the price, yet few named it as an influence. A ('deliberately') contradicts this. B: no nonexpert comparison is given in the passage, and in the actual Northcraft & Neale study amateurs were similarly affected. D is unsupported. Fact check: Northcraft & Neale (1987) matches the passage (agents toured the house, the packet's listing price was varied, appraisals were biased toward it, and few cited the listing price).

R063-05.notes: 'So crude an influence' means simple and unsophisticated. D ('approximate') is the strongest distractor, since 'crude estimate' is a common idiom, but here 'crude' modifies 'influence', not an estimate. A and C are other senses of the word. 'Unrefined, like oil' is an unusual way to word a distractor but is not defective.

R063-06.notes: Near-verbatim from P4. A twists the agents detail. B contradicts 'need not be believed'. C overstates 'done little' into 'makes worse'.

R063-07.notes: Applies P5's 'generate their own estimate before seeing any number'. B (warning) is said to do little. C keeps the person focused on the anchor. D: per P3, experts are anchored too. The best case for a distractor is B, because 'sellers' prices run high' gives a directional reason the anchor may be wrong, close to consider-the-opposite. But it is framed as a warning, which P4 explicitly discounts, and A tracks the text directly. Single best answer.

R063-08.notes: P4 opens with 'difficult to resist not because ... careless but because...'. A describes P3 and B describes P5. D reverses the text.

R063-09.notes: Explicit in P3. A detail item that heavily overlaps the setup of R063-04, but it is not defective.

R063-10.notes: Supported by P4 ('correction starts from the anchor itself') and P5 ('less in trying harder'). D overstates, since the passage never says effort worsens the bias. C is false because effort is discussed. A is the opposite. 'Skeptical' fits the measured tone, with no hostility.

passage_fact_check: Accurate: T&K 1974 (wheel 0-100 rigged to 10 or 65, the UN African-countries question, medians 25 and 45); anchoring as insufficient adjustment; Northcraft & Neale 1987; the limited effect of warnings (e.g., Wilson et al. 1996); consider-the-opposite (Mussweiler, Strack & Pfeiffer 2000). The claim that self-generated estimates reduce anchoring is a reasonable simplification. 'Before deliberate reasoning begins' is the author's interpretation and is presented as such.
